bar.title: OS Museum
intro.eyebrow: Four real computers · in your browser
intro.title: The OS Museum
intro.lede: No screenshots, no videos. Each tab is a whole x86 PC — CPU, memory, graphics card and hard disk — emulated in WebAssembly, running real machine code one instruction at a time. Switch machines whenever you like; your progress stays in your browser.
notes.title: How to use
notes.mouse.v: Click the screen and the computer takes over your mouse and keyboard. Press Esc to get the mouse back.
notes.keys.v: Your own computer grabs combinations like Ctrl + Alt + Del, Win and Alt + Tab first. Send them with the buttons below the screen instead.
notes.save.v: Switching machines or leaving the tab saves automatically, in your browser (IndexedDB) — nothing is uploaded. “Start over” takes you back to a fresh boot.
notes.net.v: None of these computers is connected to the internet, so web browsers inside them won't load pages.
notes.perf.v: Emulating a whole PC is hard work for your CPU. Desktop Chrome, Edge and Firefox run it best. Phones can boot them, but they're awkward to use.
credits.engine: The emulator is v86 (BSD-2-Clause, by Fabian Hemmer and contributors); the BIOS is SeaBIOS (LGPL-3.0). The disk images are the pre-installed builds from the v86 project. Each operating system is distributed under its own license — source links are in each machine's notes.

os.haiku.tagline: BeOS didn't die — it changed its name to Haiku
os.haiku.body: In the 1990s, BeOS was famous for its media performance and its thoroughly multithreaded design. In 1996 Apple nearly bought it to become the next Mac OS, then chose NeXT instead. After Be Inc. folded, a group of developers began rewriting it from scratch in 2001, aiming to run BeOS programs unchanged. More than twenty years on, Haiku is still under development, with its own kernel and its own UI toolkit — one of the few living desktop systems that belongs to neither the Unix nor the Windows family.
os.haiku.tips: The Deskbar in the top-right corner is the start menu; every app lives there.
Besides the built-in WebPositive browser and media player, this machine has ArtPaint, Paladin IDE, BeLife and NetHack installed — and gcc and Python 3 in the Terminal.
Window titles are little yellow tabs. Hold the Win key and drag one tab onto another window to stack or tile them (Stack & Tile).
os.reactos.tagline: Windows without a single line of Microsoft code
os.reactos.body: ReactOS aims to run Windows programs and drivers as they are, without using any Microsoft source code: everything is reimplemented from public documentation and observed behaviour — a clean-room implementation. The project has been going since 1998, and its look is frozen in the Windows 2000 and XP era. It is still alpha software and occasionally crashes, which is part of the exhibit too.
os.reactos.tips: The start menu is in the bottom-left corner; it feels almost exactly like Windows XP.
CPU-Z, gVim, HxD and OllyDbg on the desktop are the original Windows programs, running unmodified.
There's also DLX Linux (Bochs) on the desktop: an emulated PC running inside this emulated PC.
Send Ctrl + Alt + Del with the button below the screen — your own computer would catch the real keys first.
os.serenity.lineage: A whole system, written from scratch
os.serenity.tagline: A love letter to the '90s desktop
os.serenity.body: SerenityOS is an operating system Andreas Kling started writing in 2018. It looks like a late-'90s desktop, but the kernel, the GUI, the file manager — even the web browser — are all written from scratch, with almost no third-party libraries. Its browser later spun off as the Ladybird project. SerenityOS has since become 64-bit only; this is a build from back when it still supported 32-bit PCs.
os.serenity.tips: Every app is in the Serenity menu in the bottom-left corner.
Games has a dozen titles — Minesweeper, Solitaire, Chess, 2048, Flappy Bug and more — all written in-house.
The Browser on the desktop is the ancestor of what became the Ladybird browser.
os.linux.tagline: One 50 MB CD, one complete desktop
os.linux.body: Linux is the kernel Linus Torvalds started writing in 1991; today it runs everything from phones and routers to supercomputers. To keep things smooth inside a browser, this machine runs SliTaz, a distribution famous for being tiny: the whole image is under 60 MB and loads entirely into memory at boot, yet it has a full windowed desktop, a file manager, a terminal and a text editor.
os.linux.tips: Applications, at the left end of the top panel, is the program menu; right-clicking the desktop gives you another.
In the terminal you are the regular user tux. Type su with the password root to become the administrator. If you break something, hit “Start over”.
SliTaz is a live system: the entire root filesystem lives in memory. Saving works here because the memory gets saved along with it.
